record.paper_title: Causal Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Review and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can the causal-game concept of a causal Nash equilibrium, in which cooperative agents jointly optimize their actions while maintaining probabilistic beliefs about possible causal models of the environment, be applied to multi-agent reinforcement-learning problems?

evidence.quote: The Bayesian approach leads to a rational decision making criterion, where agents hold probabilistic beliefs about possible causal models of the environment. The game theoretic approach leads to the concept of a causal Nash equilibrium, where cooperative agents jointly optimise their actions. The authors feel this is an unexplored and ripe opportunity for application to the MARL problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-agent reinforcement-learning setting in which a finite set of cooperative agents repeatedly interact with an unknown environment. The environment is modeled by an unknown structural causal model drawn from a class M of candidate causal models over the variables describing states, actions, and rewards. Each agent i maintains a (possibly shared) Bayesian posterior belief b ∈ Δ(M) over which causal model in M generates the environment's transitions and rewards, updated from observed trajectories.

A causal game is defined as the tuple (N, M, b, {A_i}, {U_i}), where N is the set of agents, A_i is agent i's action space, and U_i(a, m) is agent i's expected utility under joint action a = (a_1, …, a_n) when the true causal model is m ∈ M. A joint (possibly mixed) strategy π* = (π_1*, …, π_n*) is called a causal Nash equilibrium with respect to b if, for every agent i and every alternative strategy π_i,
    E_{m ∼ b} E_{a ∼ (π_i, π_{-i}*)}[U_i(a, m)] ≤ E_{m ∼ b} E_{a ∼ π*}[U_i(a, m)],
i.e. no agent gains by unilaterally deviating, where expectations are taken jointly over the belief over causal models and the induced action distributions. In the cooperative case, U_i ≡ U is shared, and agents jointly optimize the belief-averaged utility.

Problem: Develop a multi-agent reinforcement-learning framework that operationalizes the causal Nash equilibrium concept above. Specifically:
(a) Define a learning protocol under which cooperative agents interact with an environment whose causal model is unknown, update a posterior b_t over M, and adapt joint policies π_t.
(b) Provide conditions on M, the exploration mechanism, and belief-updating rule under which π_t converges (in an appropriate sense) to a causal Nash equilibrium with respect to the limiting belief.
(c) Quantify how the resulting equilibrium policies differ — in sample complexity, robustness to model misspecification, and achieved cooperative utility — from policies learned by standard MARL algorithms that ignore causal structure.
artifact.status_search_result: A literature search for "causal Nash equilibrium" applied to multi-agent reinforcement learning returns only general work on Nash equilibria in MARL and on causality-aware single-agent or cooperative MARL methods; no published framework instantiates the Bayesian-causal-game causal Nash equilibrium concept as a learning algorithm with convergence guarantees in MARL. The direction appears to remain an open research problem.

status_evidence.title: Game Theory and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: From Nash Equilibria to Evolutionary Dynamics
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of Nash-equilibrium-based MARL and evolutionary dynamics; does not address causal-model uncertainty or causal Nash equilibria.
status_evidence.claim: Recent surveys of Nash equilibria in MARL do not include a causal-game / causal Nash equilibrium formulation.

status_evidence.title: Equilibrium Selection for Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning: A Unified Framework
status_evidence.snippet: MARL converges to Nash or related equilibria that are often non-unique; framework focuses on equilibrium selection without causal-model belief.
status_evidence.claim: State-of-the-art MARL equilibrium frameworks do not yet incorporate Bayesian beliefs over causal models.
